When I am having a talk with a Christian about religion (whether its a debate or an argument) I always notice they never seem to realize that saying "I believe in God" is not justifiable, when presented with the question "Which God" they answer 99% of the time is "God". They don't seem to realize "God" is not one being, the definition of God is the creator and ruler of the universe and source of all moral authority; the supreme being.. They never understand the fact that each religion (for the most part) has their particular God and most of the time those God's contradict other God's existences, so which God is it? Maybe none.
Something I noticed during religious talks with Christians...

There are actually people who think that all religions (well, at least all monotheistic religions) are talking about the same god. This view is probably not compatible with hardcore Christian viewpoint (the Bible is the ultimate truth, everything that contradicts it is a lie), but many people have a slightly lighter philosophy - Christians got something right, while Muslim got other things about God right. I don't think this point of view is self-contradictory.

But I'm with you. I also like asking the "which god" question. Humans made up so many gods it's nice to specify which one you're talking about. Yes, I know, you are talking about one true god, but who is he (she, it, they)? Zeus? Ra? Jesus?

In the street epistemology video's of Anthony most Christians seem offended when he asks them which god it is they believe. It really strikes me as odd, it happened exclusively with Christians. I guess its because they live in a predominantly Cristian country, I am from Holland where Atheism is the norm.
I just don't see the point in arguing, or even debating, with someone who believes in an invisible overlord. Logic isn't going to convince someone who openly embraces illogic.

Christians put a lot of emphasis on their god being the only god, and that anything other than theirs is simply wrong. The Nicene Creed (which I still have memorized from my years as a Catholic) begins with the line "I believe in one God, the Father the Almighty, the maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible." In Catholicism (and Christianity as a whole, for the most part), the Christian god is the only god.

When a monotheistic has a God with no name -it increases the gods ambiguity. Suddenly it's easier for them to imagine their God however they want, because it doesn't even have a name, or even a face really.

Monotheistic religions by definition believe that there is only a single god, ever and always.

Expecting them to "allow" for the existence of other gods is entirely unrealistic. If they are able to understand that other cultures had other god(s) that they believed in as much as christians do their god they are far less indoctrinated than most.
